title: Chapter 36. Of the Word of God, and of Prophets
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth
paragraphs: When there is mention of the word of God, or of man, it does not signify a part of speech such as grammarians call a noun or a verb, or any simple sound without a context of other words to make it meaningful, but a perfect speech or discourse by which the speaker affirms, denies, commands, promises, threatens, wishes, or asks. In this sense it is not vocabulum that means a word, but sermo (in Greek logos) — some speech, discourse, or saying.

Again, when we say 'the word of God,' or 'of man,' it may sometimes be understood of the speaker (as the words that God has spoken, or that a man has spoken). In that sense, when we say 'the Gospel of St Matthew,' we understand St Matthew to be the writer of it. And sometimes it is understood of the subject: in this sense, when we read in the Bible 'The words of the days of the kings of Israel, or of Judah,' it is meant that the acts done in those days were the subject of those 'words.' And in the Greek, which (in Scripture) retains many Hebraisms, by 'the word of God' is often meant not what is spoken by God, but what is spoken concerning God, and his government — that is, the doctrine of religion. So much so that to say logos theou and theologia is all one — which is the doctrine we usually call divinity, as is plain from the following passages. Acts 13:46: 'Then Paul and Barnabas grew bold, and said: It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you; but seeing you put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.' What is here called the word of God was the doctrine of the Christian religion, as is evident from what goes before. And in Acts 5:20, where it is said to the apostles by an angel, 'Go, stand and speak in the temple, all the words of this life' — by 'the words of this life' is meant the doctrine of the gospel, as is evident from what they did in the temple, and is expressed in the last verse of the same chapter: 'Daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Christ Jesus.' From this it is plain that Jesus Christ was the subject of this 'word of life,' or (which is all one) the subject of the 'words of this life eternal' that our Saviour offered them. So (Acts 15:7) the word of God is called the word of the gospel, because it contains the doctrine of the kingdom of Christ; and the same word (Rom. 10:8–9) is called the word of faith — that is, as is there explained, the doctrine of Christ come, and raised from the dead. Also (Matt. 13:19): 'When any one hears the word of the kingdom,' that is, the doctrine of the kingdom taught by Christ. Again, the same word is said (Acts 12:24) to 'grow and to be multiplied'; which to understand of the evangelical doctrine is easy, but of the voice or speech of God, hard and strange. In the same sense the 'doctrine of devils' signifies not the words of any devil, but the doctrine of heathen men concerning daemons, and those phantasms which they worshipped as gods (1 Tim. 4:1).

Considering these two meanings of the WORD OF GOD as it is taken in Scripture, it is plain in this latter sense (where it is taken for the doctrine of the Christian religion) that the whole Scripture is the word of God; but in the former sense not so. For example, though the words 'I am the Lord your God, etc.' to the end of the Ten Commandments were spoken by God to Moses, the preface 'God spoke these words and said' is to be understood as the words of the one who wrote the holy history. The word of God, as it is taken for what he has spoken, is understood sometimes properly, sometimes metaphorically. Properly, as the words he has spoken to his prophets; metaphorically, for his wisdom, power, and eternal decree in making the world — in which sense, those Fiats, 'Let there be light,' 'Let there be a firmament,' 'Let us make man,' and so on (Genesis 1), are the word of God. And in the same sense it is said (John 1:3) that 'all things were made by it, and without it was nothing made that was made'; and (Heb. 1:3) 'He upholds all things by the word of his power' — that is, by the power of his word, that is, by his power; and (Heb. 11:3) 'The worlds were framed by the word of God'; and many other passages to the same sense. So also among the Latins, the name 'fate,' which means properly the word spoken, is taken in the same sense.

Second, for the effect of his word — that is, for the thing itself which by his word is affirmed, commanded, threatened, or promised. As in Psalm 105:19, where Joseph is said to have been kept in prison 'till his word was come' — that is, till what he had (Gen. 40:13) foretold to Pharaoh's butler, concerning his being restored to his office, had come to pass. There, 'his word was come' means the thing itself had come to pass. So also (1 Kings 18:36) Elijah says to God, 'I have done all these your words,' instead of 'I have done all these things at your word,' or commandment. And (Jer. 17:15), 'Where is the word of the Lord?' is put for 'Where is the evil he threatened?' And (Ezek. 12:28), 'There shall none of my words be prolonged any more' — by 'words' are meant the things God promised to his people. And in the New Testament (Matt. 24:35), 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away' — that is, there is nothing I have promised or foretold that shall not come to pass. And in this sense it is that St John the Evangelist — and, I think, St John alone — calls our Saviour himself, in the flesh, 'the Word of God,' as in John 1:14: 'The Word was made flesh.' That is, the word, or promise, that Christ should come into the world, 'who in the beginning was with God' — that is, it was in the purpose of God the Father to send God the Son into the world, to enlighten men in the way of eternal life; but it was not till then put into execution, and actually incarnate. So our Saviour is there called 'the Word' not because he was the promise, but the thing promised. Those who, taking occasion from this passage, commonly call him 'the Verbum of God,' do but render the text more obscure. They might as well call him the noun of God: for by noun, as also by verb, men understand nothing but a part of speech, a voice, a sound, that neither affirms nor denies, nor commands nor promises, nor is any substance corporeal or spiritual; and therefore it cannot be said to be either God or man — whereas our Saviour is both. And this Word, which St John in his Gospel says was with God, is (in his First Epistle, verse 1) called 'the Word of life'; and (verse 2) 'the eternal life, which was with the Father.' So he can in no other sense be called the Word than in the sense in which he is called eternal life — that is, 'he who has procured us eternal life,' by his coming in the flesh. So also (Revelation 19:13) the Apostle, speaking of Christ clothed in a garment dipped in blood, says his name is 'the Word of God' — which is to be understood as if he had said his name had been 'He that has come according to the purpose of God from the beginning, and according to his word and promises delivered by the prophets.' So there is nothing here of the incarnation of a Word, but of the incarnation of God the Son — therefore called the Word, because his incarnation was the performance of the promise; just as the Holy Ghost is called the Promise (Acts 1:4; Luke 24:49).

There are also passages of Scripture where, by the word of God, are signified such words as are consonant with reason and equity, though spoken sometimes neither by a prophet, nor by a holy man. For Pharaoh Necho was an idolater; yet his words to the good King Josiah, in which he advised him by messengers not to oppose his march against Carchemish, are said to have proceeded from the mouth of God; and that Josiah, not heeding them, was slain in the battle — as may be read in 2 Chron. 35:21–23. It is true that, as the same history is related in the first book of Esdras, it was not Pharaoh but Jeremiah who spoke these words to Josiah from the mouth of the Lord. But we are to give credit to the canonical Scripture, whatever is written in the Apocrypha.

The word of God is also to be taken for the dictates of reason and equity, when the same is said in the Scriptures to be written in man's heart; as in Psalm 36:31; Jeremiah 31:33; Deuteronomy 30:11, 14; and many other like passages.

The name PROPHET signifies in Scripture sometimes Prolocutor — that is, one who speaks from God to man, or from man to God; and sometimes Praedictor, or foreteller of things to come; and sometimes one who speaks incoherently, as men who are distracted. It is most frequently used in the sense of speaking from God to the people. So Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others were prophets. And in this sense the high priest was a prophet, for he alone went into the Sanctum Sanctorum to inquire of God, and was to declare God's answer to the people. So when Caiaphas said it was expedient that one man should die for the people, St John says (chapter 11:51) that 'he spoke not this of himself, but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that one man should die for the nation.' Also those who in Christian congregations taught the people (1 Cor. 14:3) are said to prophesy. In the like sense it is that God says to Moses (Exod. 4:16), concerning Aaron, 'He shall be your spokesman to the people; and he shall be to you a mouth, and you shall be to him in the place of God' — and what here is 'spokesman' is (chapter 7:1) interpreted as 'prophet': 'See (says God) I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.' In the sense of speaking from man to God, Abraham is called a prophet (Gen. 20:7), where God in a dream speaks to Abimelech in this way: 'Now therefore restore the man his wife, for he is a prophet, and shall pray for you' — whereby it may also be gathered that the name of prophet may not improperly be given to those who in Christian churches have a calling to say public prayers for the congregation. In the same sense, the prophets who came down from the high place (or hill of God) with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp (1 Sam. 10:5–6), and (verse 10) Saul among them, are said to prophesy, in that they praised God in that way publicly. In the like sense, Miriam is called a prophetess (Exod. 15:20). So it is also to be taken in 1 Cor. 11:4–5, where St Paul says, 'Every man that prays or prophesies with his head covered, etc., and every woman that prays or prophesies with her head uncovered' — for 'prophecy' in that place signifies nothing more than praising God in psalms and holy songs, which women might do in the church, though it were not lawful for them to speak to the congregation. And in this signification it is that the poets of the heathen, who composed hymns and other sorts of poems in honour of their gods, were called vates (prophets), as is well enough known by all who are versed in the books of the Gentiles, and as is evident in Titus 1:12, where St Paul says of the Cretans that a prophet of their own said they were liars — not that St Paul held their poets for prophets, but acknowledges that the word 'prophet' was commonly used to signify those who celebrated the honour of God in verse.

When by prophecy is meant prediction, or foretelling of future contingents, not only were those prophets who were God's spokesmen and foretold to others what God had foretold to them, but so also were all those impostors who claim by the help of familiar spirits, or by superstitious divination from past events with false causes, to foretell similar events in time to come; of which (as I have already declared in the 12th chapter of this discourse) there are many kinds, and who gain, in the opinion of the common sort of men, a greater reputation for prophecy by one chance event that may be wrested to their purpose than can be lost again by any number of failings. Prophecy is not an art, nor (when taken for prediction) a constant vocation, but an extraordinary and temporary employment from God, most often of good men, but sometimes also of the wicked. The woman of Endor, who is said to have had a familiar spirit, and thereby to have raised a phantasm of Samuel and foretold Saul his death, was not therefore a prophetess; for she had no science by which she could raise such a phantasm, nor does it appear that God commanded the raising of it. He only guided that imposture to be a means of Saul's terror and discouragement, and consequently of the rout by which he fell. And for incoherent speech, it was among the Gentiles taken for one kind of prophecy, because the prophets of their oracles, intoxicated with a spirit, or vapour from the cave of the Pythian oracle at Delphi, were for the time really mad, and spoke like madmen; out of whose loose words a sense might be made to fit any event, in such a way as all bodies are said to be made of materia prima. In Scripture I find it also so taken (1 Sam. 18:10) in these words: 'And the evil spirit came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of the house.'

And although there are so many meanings of the word 'prophet' in Scripture, the most frequent is that in which it is taken for the one to whom God speaks immediately what the prophet is to say from him, to some other man, or to the people. And on this a question may be asked: in what manner does God speak to such a prophet? Can it (some may say) be properly said that God has voice and language, when it cannot be properly said that he has a tongue, or other organs, as a man? The prophet David argues in this way: 'Shall he that made the eye not see? Or he that made the ear not hear?' But this may be spoken, not (as usually) to signify God's nature, but to signify our intention to honour him. For 'to see' and 'to hear' are honourable attributes, and may be given to God, to declare (as far as our capacity can conceive) his almighty power. But if it were taken in the strict and proper sense, one might argue, from his making of all parts of man's body, that he also has the same use of them that we have; which would be many of them so unseemly that it would be the greatest contumely in the world to ascribe them to him. We are therefore to interpret God's speaking to men immediately as the way (whatever it is) by which God makes them understand his will. And the ways by which he does this are many, and to be sought only in Holy Scripture. There, though many times it is said that God spoke to this or that person, without declaring in what manner, there are again many places that also give the signs by which they were to acknowledge his presence and commandment; and by these may be understood how he spoke to many of the rest.

In what manner God spoke to Adam, and Eve, and Cain, and Noah, is not expressed; nor how he spoke to Abraham, until the time when he came out of his own country to Shechem in the land of Canaan; and then (Gen. 12:7) God is said to have appeared to him. So there is one way by which God made his presence manifest: by an apparition, or vision. And again (Gen. 15:1), the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision — that is, something, as a sign of God's presence, appeared as God's messenger, to speak to him. Again, the Lord appeared to Abraham (Gen. 18:1) by an apparition of three angels; and to Abimelech (Gen. 20:3) in a dream; to Lot (Gen. 19:1) by an apparition of two angels; and to Hagar (Gen. 21:17) by the apparition of one angel; and to Abraham again (Gen. 22:11) by the apparition of a voice from heaven; and (Gen. 26:24) to Isaac in the night (that is, in his sleep, or by a dream); and to Jacob (Gen. 28:12) in a dream — that is (in the words of the text), 'Jacob dreamed that he saw a ladder, etc.' And (Gen. 32:1) in a vision of angels. And to Moses (Exod. 3:2) in the apparition of a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. And after the time of Moses, wherever the manner in which God spoke directly to a man in the Old Testament is expressed, he always spoke by a vision, or by a dream — as to Gideon, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the rest of the prophets; and often in the New Testament, as to Joseph, to St Peter, to St Paul, and to St John the Evangelist in the Apocalypse.

Only to Moses did he speak in a more extraordinary manner, on Mount Sinai and in the tabernacle; and to the high priest in the tabernacle, and in the Sanctum Sanctorum of the temple. But Moses, and after him the high priests, were prophets of a more eminent place and degree in God's favour. And God himself in express words declares that to other prophets he spoke in dreams and visions, but to his servant Moses, in such a manner as a man speaks to his friend. The words are these (Numb. 12:6–8): 'If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known to him in a vision, and will speak to him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all my house; with him I will speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the Lord shall he behold.' And (Exod. 33:11), 'The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.' And yet this speaking of God to Moses was by the mediation of an angel, or angels, as appears expressly in Acts 7:35 and 53 and in Gal. 3:19; and was therefore a vision, though a clearer vision than was given to other prophets. And in keeping with this, where God says (Deut. 13:1), 'If there arise among you a prophet, or dreamer of dreams,' the latter word is only the interpretation of the former. And (Joel 2:28), 'Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions' — where again, the word 'prophecy' is expounded by 'dream' and 'vision.' And in the same way it was that God spoke to Solomon, promising him wisdom, riches, and honour; for the text says (1 Kings 3:15), 'And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream.' So that generally the prophets extraordinary in the Old Testament took notice of the word of God in no other way than from their dreams or visions — that is, from the imaginings they had in their sleep, or in an ecstasy. Which imaginings, in every true prophet, were supernatural; but in false prophets were either natural, or feigned.

The same prophets were nevertheless said to speak by the Spirit — as in Zechariah 7:12, where the prophet, speaking of the Jews, says: 'They made their hearts hard as adamant, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the Lord of hosts has sent in his Spirit by the former prophets.' By which it is plain that speaking by the Spirit, or inspiration, was not a particular manner of God's speaking, different from vision; when those who were said to speak by the Spirit were extraordinary prophets, such as had to have, for every new message, a particular commission — or (what is all one) a new dream, or vision.

To prophets of perpetual calling, and supreme, God spoke in the Old Testament from the mercy seat, in a manner not expressed in the Scripture. Of prophets who were so by a perpetual calling in the Old Testament, some were supreme and some subordinate. The supreme were first Moses; and after him the high priest, each one for his time, as long as the priesthood was royal. And after the people of the Jews had rejected God, that he should no more reign over them, those kings who submitted themselves to God's government were also his chief prophets; and the high priest's office became ministerial. When God was to be consulted, they put on the holy vestments and inquired of the Lord, as the king commanded them, and were deprived of their office when the king thought fit. For King Saul (1 Sam. 13:9) commanded the burnt offering to be brought; and (1 Sam. 14:18) he commands the priest to bring the ark near him, and (verse 19) again to let it alone, because he saw an advantage over his enemies. And in the same chapter Saul asks counsel of God. In the same way King David, after his being anointed, though before he had possession of the kingdom, is said to 'inquire of the Lord' (1 Sam. 23:2) whether he should fight against the Philistines at Keilah; and (verse 10) David commands the priest to bring him the ephod, to inquire whether he should stay in Keilah, or not. And King Solomon (1 Kings 2:27) took the priesthood from Abiathar, and gave it (verse 35) to Zadok. So Moses, and the high priests, and the pious kings who inquired of God on all extraordinary occasions how they were to conduct themselves, or what outcome they were to have, were all sovereign prophets. But in what manner God spoke to them is not plain. To say that when Moses went up to God on Mount Sinai, it was a dream, or vision, such as other prophets had, is contrary to the distinction God made between Moses and other prophets (Numb. 12:6–8). To say God spoke or appeared as he is in his own nature is to deny his infiniteness, invisibility, incomprehensibility. To say he spoke by inspiration, or infusion, of the Holy Spirit — as the Holy Spirit signifies the Deity — is to make Moses equal with Christ, in whom alone the Godhead (as St Paul says, Col. 2:9) 'dwells bodily.' And lastly, to say he spoke by the Holy Spirit, as it signifies the graces or gifts of the Holy Spirit, is to attribute nothing supernatural to him. For God disposes men to piety, justice, mercy, truth, faith, and every kind of virtue — moral and intellectual — by doctrine, example, and various occasions, natural and ordinary.

And as these ways cannot be applied to God in his speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai, so they cannot be applied to him in his speaking to the high priests from the mercy seat. So in what manner God spoke to those sovereign prophets of the Old Testament, whose office it was to inquire of him, is not intelligible. In the time of the New Testament there was no sovereign prophet but our Saviour, who was both God who spoke, and the prophet to whom he spoke.

To prophets of perpetual calling but subordinate, God spoke by the Spirit. To subordinate prophets of perpetual calling, I find no place that proves God spoke to them supernaturally, but only in such a manner as he naturally inclines men to piety, to belief, to righteousness, and to other virtues — all other Christian men. Which way, though it consists in constitution, instruction, education, and the occasions and inducements men have to Christian virtues, is yet truly attributed to the operation of the Spirit of God, or the Holy Spirit (which in our language we call the Holy Ghost); for there is no good inclination that is not from the operation of God. But these operations are not always supernatural. So when a prophet is said to speak in the Spirit, or by the Spirit of God, we are to understand no more than that he speaks according to God's will, declared by the supreme prophet. For the most common acceptation of the word 'spirit' is in the sense of a man's intention, mind, or disposition.

In the time of Moses there were seventy men besides himself who prophesied in the camp of the Israelites. In what manner God spoke to them is declared in Numbers 11:25: 'The Lord came down in a cloud, and spoke to Moses, and took of the spirit that was upon him, and gave it to the seventy elders. And it came to pass, when the spirit rested on them, they prophesied, and did not cease.' By which it is plain, first, that their prophesying to the people was subservient and subordinate to the prophesying of Moses; for God took of the spirit of Moses to put on them, so that they prophesied as Moses would have them — otherwise they had not been allowed to prophesy at all. For there was (verse 27) a complaint made against them to Moses, and Joshua would have had Moses forbid them; which Moses did not, but said to Joshua, 'Be not jealous on my behalf.' Second, that the Spirit of God in that place signifies nothing but the mind and disposition to obey, and to assist Moses, in the administration of the government. For if it were meant that they had the substantial Spirit of God — that is, the divine nature, inspired into them — then they had it no less than Christ himself, in whom alone the Spirit of God dwelt bodily. It is meant therefore of the gift and grace of God, that guided them to co-operate with Moses, from whom their spirit was derived. And it appears (verse 16) that they were such as Moses himself should appoint for elders and officers of the people; for the words are, 'Gather to me seventy men, whom you know to be elders and officers of the people' — where 'you know' is the same as 'you appoint,' or 'have appointed to be such.' For we are told before (Exod. 18) that Moses, following the counsel of Jethro his father-in-law, appointed judges and officers over the people, such as feared God; and of these were those seventy whom God, by putting Moses' spirit on them, inclined to aid Moses in the administration of the kingdom. And in this sense the Spirit of God is said (1 Sam. 16:13–14), immediately on the anointing of David, to have come on David, and left Saul — God giving his graces to him whom he chose to govern his people, and taking them away from the one he rejected. So that by 'the Spirit' is meant inclination to God's service, and not any supernatural revelation.

God also spoke many times by the outcome of lots, which were ordered by such as he had put in authority over his people. So we read that God made known, by the lots Saul caused to be drawn (1 Sam. 14:43), the fault that Jonathan had committed in eating a honeycomb, contrary to the oath taken by the people. And (Josh. 18:10), God divided the land of Canaan among the Israelites by the 'lots that Joshua cast before the Lord in Shiloh.' In the same way it seems to be that God discovered (Joshua 7:16, etc.) the crime of Achan. And these are the ways by which God declared his will in the Old Testament.

All these ways he used also in the New Testament. To the Virgin Mary, by a vision of an angel; to Joseph in a dream; again to Paul on the way to Damascus, in a vision of our Saviour; and to Peter in the vision of a sheet let down from heaven with various sorts of flesh, of clean and unclean beasts, and in prison by the vision of an angel; and to all the apostles, and writers of the New Testament, by the graces of his Spirit; and to the apostles again (at the choosing of Matthias in the place of Judas Iscariot) by lot.

Since then all prophecy supposes vision, or dream (which two, when they are natural, are the same), or some special gift of God so rarely seen in mankind as to be admired where seen; and since both such gifts and the most extraordinary dreams and visions may proceed from God, not only by his supernatural and immediate operation, but also by his natural operation, and through the mediation of secondary causes — there is need of reason and judgement to discern between natural and supernatural gifts, and between natural and supernatural visions or dreams. And consequently men have need to be very circumspect and wary in obeying the voice of a man who, claiming to be a prophet, requires us to obey God in the way that he, in God's name, tells us is the way to happiness. For he who claims to teach men the way to so great a felicity claims to govern them — that is, to rule and reign over them; which is a thing that all men naturally desire, and is therefore to be suspected of ambition and imposture; and consequently ought to be examined, and tested, by every man before he yields them obedience — unless he has yielded it to them already, in the institution of a commonwealth, as when the prophet is the civil sovereign, or is authorised by the civil sovereign. And if this examination of prophets and spirits were not allowed to every one of the people, it would have been to no purpose to set out the marks by which every man might be able to distinguish between those he ought, and those he ought not, to follow. Since therefore such marks are set out (Deut. 13:1ff.) to know a prophet by, and (1 John 4:1ff.) to know a spirit by; and since there is so much prophesying in the Old Testament, and so much preaching in the New Testament against prophets; and so much greater a number ordinarily of false prophets than of true — every one is to beware of obeying their directions, at his own peril. And first, that there were many more false than true prophets appears from this, that when Ahab (1 Kings 22 [which Hobbes here numbers as 12]) consulted four hundred prophets, they were all false impostors, except only one — Micaiah. And a little before the time of the captivity, the prophets were generally liars. 'The prophets,' says the Lord through Jeremiah 14:14, 'prophesy lies in my name. I sent them not, neither have I commanded them, nor spoken to them; they prophesy to you a false vision, a thing of naught, and the deceit of their heart.' So much so that God commanded the people, by the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah (chapter 23:16), not to obey them: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: listen not to the words of the prophets that prophesy to you. They make you vain; they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the Lord.'

Since, then, there was in the time of the Old Testament such quarrelling among the visionary prophets — one contesting with another, and asking 'When did the Spirit depart from me, to go to you?' as between Micaiah and the rest of the four hundred; and such giving of the lie to one another (as in Jeremiah 14:14); and such controversies, in the New Testament and at this day, among the spiritual prophets — every man then was, and now is, bound to make use of his natural reason, to apply to all prophecy the rules God has given us to discern the true from the false. Of which rules, in the Old Testament one was the conformity of doctrine to what Moses the sovereign prophet had taught them, and the other the miraculous power of foretelling what God would bring to pass, as I have already shown out of Deut. 13:1ff. And in the New Testament there was only one mark, and that was the preaching of this doctrine: that Jesus is the Christ — that is, the king of the Jews, promised in the Old Testament. Whoever denied that article was a false prophet, whatever miracles he might seem to work; and he who taught it was a true prophet. For St John (1 Epistle 4:2ff.), speaking expressly of the means to examine spirits, whether they are of God or not — after he has told them that there would arise false prophets — says: 'Hereby know the Spirit of God. Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God' — that is, is approved and allowed as a prophet of God; not that he is a godly man, or one of the elect, just because he confesses, professes, or preaches Jesus to be the Christ, but that he is an avowed prophet. For God sometimes speaks by prophets whose persons he has not accepted, as he did by Balaam; and as he foretold Saul of his death, by the witch of Endor. Again in the next verse: 'Every spirit that confesses not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh, is not of Christ. And this is the spirit of antichrist.' So the rule is perfect on both sides: that he is a true prophet who preaches the Messiah already come, in the person of Jesus; and a false one who denies him come, and looks for him in some future impostor who will take that honour on himself falsely — whom the apostle there properly calls antichrist. Every man therefore ought to consider who is the sovereign prophet — that is, who it is that is God's viceregent on earth, and has, next under God, the authority of governing Christian men; and to observe as a rule that doctrine which, in the name of God, he commands to be taught; and by this to examine and try out the truth of those doctrines which pretended prophets, with miracles or without, may at any time advance. And if they find it contrary to that rule, to do as those did who came to Moses and complained that there were some who prophesied in the camp, whose authority so to do they doubted; and leave it to the sovereign, as they did to Moses, to uphold them or to forbid them as he shall see cause; and if he disavows them, then no more to obey their voice; or if he approves them, then to obey them, as men to whom God has given a part of the spirit of their sovereign. For when Christian men do not take their Christian sovereign for God's prophet, they must either take their own dreams for the prophecy they mean to be governed by, and the swelling of their own hearts for the Spirit of God; or they must suffer themselves to be led by some strange prince, or by some of their fellow subjects, that can bewitch them, by slander of the government, into rebellion, without other miracle to confirm their calling than sometimes an extraordinary success, and impunity. And by this means, destroying all laws both divine and human, they reduce all order, government, and society to the first chaos of violence and civil war.
